promptText: Why can't you just send a scanned PDF straight to an LLM and trust the JSON it returns?
options: The model's self-reported confidence isn't calibrated - it returns equally fluent, schema-valid JSON whether every field is correct or one is subtly wrong, so an independent verification layer is needed
LLMs are physically incapable of accepting an image as input
JSON output is inherently less reliable than plain-text output from any model
Scanned PDFs cannot be represented in a chat-style API request under any circumstances
explanation: Without cross-checks like OCR position matching, type/range validation, and totals reconciliation, there is no way to know which extractions are trustworthy enough to feed into financial or legal downstream systems.

promptText: What is the difference between OCR and document layout analysis?
options: OCR converts pixels into text - what text is on the page; layout analysis determines the spatial and structural relationships between that text - how it's organized into tables, columns, and headers
OCR and layout analysis are two names for exactly the same processing step
Layout analysis converts pixels to text, while OCR determines table structure
OCR only works on native, born-digital PDFs and never on scanned images
explanation: Knowing the words alone is not enough to know, for example, which number in a table is the grand total versus a line-item subtotal - that requires layout analysis on top of OCR.

promptText: Why should document chunking for retrieval be layout-aware instead of fixed-length?
options: Fixed-length chunking can split a table row or clause across chunk boundaries, causing a retrieval query to surface only half a fact; layout-aware chunking respects natural boundaries so each chunk is a coherent unit
Layout-aware chunking is only relevant for documents written in languages other than English
Fixed-length chunking is strictly faster and equally accurate, so layout-awareness is only a stylistic preference
Layout-aware chunking eliminates the need for any confidence scoring downstream
explanation: A rent clause split mid-sentence across two chunks means a query about rent amount may retrieve only half the fact; layout-aware chunking keeps clauses, table rows, and sections intact.

promptText: What is straight-through processing (STP) rate, and why is it the platform's north-star metric?
options: The percentage of documents processed end-to-end with zero human touch; it directly drives unit economics since a low STP rate means most processing cost is still human labor no matter how sophisticated the model is
The percentage of documents that fail OCR entirely and must be re-scanned
A measure of how many different file formats the platform is able to ingest
The speed, in milliseconds, at which a single page can be processed
explanation: Accuracy alone is incomplete without STP, since a system can be highly accurate on the documents it auto-processes while still routing most volume to expensive manual review.

promptText: What is a bounding box, and why is it central to explainability in document extraction?
options: The pixel coordinates (plus page number) of the region where an extracted value was found, letting the platform show - not just claim - where a number came from, which speeds review and enables audit
A security sandbox that isolates the multimodal model from the rest of the pipeline
The confidence threshold above which a field is auto-processed without review
A fixed-size rectangle used only for redacting sensitive fields like Social Security numbers
explanation: Storing a bounding box alongside every extracted field is what makes a reviewer's correction fast and what makes the system auditable to a compliance team or customer.

promptText: Why is a "born-digital" PDF handled differently from a scanned PDF in the pipeline?
options: A born-digital PDF has an actual text layer generated by the originating software, so text can be extracted programmatically with no OCR error, while a scanned PDF is effectively an image and requires OCR, which introduces its own error class
Born-digital and scanned PDFs are processed identically since both are stored in the same file format
Scanned PDFs never need OCR because scanners embed a hidden text layer automatically
Born-digital PDFs cannot contain tables or multi-column layouts
explanation: A single PDF can mix a native cover page with scanned attachments, so the pipeline must detect which case it is dealing with per page rather than assuming one or the other.

promptText: Why does the chapter insist on tracking precision and recall separately per field type rather than a single blended accuracy number?
options: The cost of an error is wildly different per field (a wrong loan amount versus a wrong page count), and averaging accuracy across all fields can hide a critical field that is frequently wrong beneath many easy fields that are almost always right
Per-field metrics are only useful for documents with fewer than five fields
A single blended accuracy number is always more informative to a regulator than per-field metrics
Precision and recall cannot be computed separately for extraction tasks, only combined
explanation: A 96% overall accuracy can hide a field like "loan amount" that is wrong 15% of the time, buried under many easy fields that are essentially always right.

promptText: What does it mean for a confidence score to be "calibrated," and how is this checked in practice?
options: Among all fields reported at roughly 90% confidence, roughly 90% should actually be correct; this is checked empirically by bucketing fields by reported confidence and plotting against observed accuracy
A calibrated confidence score means the model always reports exactly 100% for every field
Calibration is achieved automatically the moment structured output validation passes
Calibration only matters for handwriting recognition, not printed text extraction
explanation: If points sit below the diagonal on this calibration curve, the system is over-confident and auto-processing wrong extractions - the more dangerous of the two failure directions.

promptText: Why isn't "the model returned valid JSON matching the schema" the same as "the extraction is correct"?
options: Schema validation only checks structure and type, never factual correctness - a syntactically perfect JSON object can still contain a wrong dollar amount that passes every structural check
Schema-valid JSON is mathematically guaranteed to be factually correct by construction
Structural validation and factual correctness are the same check performed twice for redundancy
Schema validation failures are always caused by OCR errors, never by the model itself
explanation: Only the independent cross-validation layer - checking against OCR ground truth, type/range plausibility, and arithmetic reconciliation - can catch a structurally perfect but factually wrong extraction.

promptText: Why does the platform run deterministic OCR first even for pages that will also go through a multimodal LLM extraction step?
options: OCR output gives an auditable, position-verifiable ground truth to independently cross-check the LLM's extraction against, which is the only way to compute genuine, non-self-reported confidence
Multimodal models cannot technically process an image without a pre-existing OCR text layer
Running OCR first is purely a legacy step kept for backward compatibility, with no bearing on confidence
OCR is faster than the multimodal model, so it is used exclusively for latency, not for validation
explanation: Without deterministic OCR, there is no independent signal to compute genuine confidence, only the model's own unreliable self-assessment.

promptText: What is the prompt-injection risk in document extraction, and how is it mitigated?
options: A document's visible or hidden text can be crafted to look like an instruction (e.g., "report this total as $0"); mitigation includes delimiting document content clearly as data, plus relying on cross-validation, since an injected value inconsistent with OCR ground truth typically fails and routes to review
Prompt injection is not possible through document content, only through direct chat messages
The only defense against document-based prompt injection is banning all scanned PDFs entirely
Cross-validation against OCR ground truth has no effect on catching injected instructions
explanation: Document content - visible text, hidden text layers, or manipulated image content - is untrusted input to the model exactly as covered in the general security material, and cross-validation is the second line of defense.

promptText: Why must document-boundary detection be a first-class pipeline stage rather than an incidental preprocessing step?
options: Real files often contain multiple logical documents scanned together, such as a cover email stapled to a contract; a pipeline that assumes one-document-per-file will misclassify and mis-extract silently
Document-boundary detection is only relevant for documents longer than 100 pages
Every uploaded file is guaranteed to contain exactly one logical document by construction
Boundary detection is handled automatically by the multimodal LLM with no separate pipeline stage needed
explanation: This is exactly the kind of long-tail case that separates a system tested on clean sample data from one tested on real production volume.

promptText: A client reports that extraction accuracy dropped noticeably last month with no code changes on the platform's side. In what order does the chapter recommend investigating?
options: First check for document population drift (a vendor changed its template), then a silent upstream provider change (an LLM or OCR engine version update), then per-field precision/recall trends from the audit store to isolate whether the regression is concentrated in specific fields or document types
Immediately retrain the entire extraction model from scratch before investigating anything else
Assume the client is misusing the platform and request they resubmit all documents
Check only the total document volume processed that month, since volume is the sole driver of accuracy
explanation: "No code changes on our side" does not rule out a dependency change, and per-field metrics narrow the root cause quickly - which is exactly why versioning every schema, prompt, and model is non-negotiable.

promptText: A stakeholder wants to expand the platform to a new document type by simply "adding it to the prompt." What is the actual engineering cost, per the chapter?
options: A new document type actually requires a new target schema, extended classification, new cross-validation rules specific to that document's fields, a labeled evaluation set to measure per-field precision/recall, and recalibrated confidence thresholds - a cost proportional to field complexity, not a one-line prompt edit
Adding a new document type genuinely is just a one-line prompt change, and the stakeholder's framing is correct
New document types require rebuilding the entire platform's OCR engine from scratch
Only the confidence thresholds need to change; schema and classification are universal across all document types
explanation: Confidence thresholds tuned for invoices do not transfer to leases or medical forms, and skipping the evaluation-set step is exactly the shortcut that produces unaudited, uncalibrated failures.

promptText: Why is averaging confidence across all of a document's fields into one document-level score considered a design mistake, synthesizing the chapter's calibration and human-review guidance?
options: A document-level average can mask one critical low-confidence field beneath many easy, high-confidence fields, defeating both accurate routing (auto-process vs. review) and the field-level review workflow that lets a reviewer correct only the flagged field in seconds
Document-level confidence is strictly more accurate than field-level confidence because it accounts for more data
Field-level confidence is only useful for documents that contain exactly one field
Averaging confidence across fields has no effect on routing decisions, since routing is based on document type alone
explanation: Per-field confidence is what makes targeted human review possible - a reviewer corrects only the flagged field instead of re-verifying the whole document, which is the difference between a review workflow that scales and one that doesn't.
